newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: European shippers offered bargain basement bunkers.
newsitem.headline: European shippers offered bargain basement bunkers.

text.p: Tumbling fuel oil prices in the last three weeks have given European shipowners bargain deals relative to crude and the indications are that the lower price regime may not be a short-term blip.
High sulphur fuel oil barges in Rotterdam, the largest bunkering port in Europe, have plummeted by almost $25 a tonne, or nearly 20 percent, since January 7.

Although crude has fallen too, the fuel oil slump is more extreme. Relative to crude, fuel oil has fallen from 63 percent to 55 percent of the price of Brent. A year ago, high sulphur fuel oil barges were trading at around 75 percent of the Brent crude price.
Many bunker suppliers, brokers and shippers are confused.
"Nobody can provide me with a sufficient answer," one supplier said.
Some refiners insist the market's recent weakness is merely the result of the herd instinct.
"The market is nothing else than the general perception," a trader at one major said.
Bunker buyers have instead said the number of ship arrivals is down, resulting in sharply lower demand for fuel oil.
"The main cause is the lack of demand. I hear the majors are especially wondering where the ships are," said one shipping operator.
However, neither view is entirely borne out by others in the market and few facts that do appear. Perhaps some bunker buyers and brokers are confused by the sudden swings from activity to torpor.
"Demand is very erratic. We have nothing one day and then 30,000 tonnes," said one supplier.

However, total demand, while slightly lower than for normal months, is typical for the time of year. Traders estimate that demand has totalled around 350,000 tonnes, compared with a normal 400-450,000 tonnes.
"There is a seasonal influence. In the last few years, we notice a dip in the amount (of vessels arriving) in the months January and February," one ARA trader said.
Utility consumption is also down. Some power companies are using gas instead and some, like Portugal's EdP, can rely on heavy rains and hydro-power.
However, the main reason for the price drop appears instead to be a rise of supply.

Stocks in the ARA area were estimated to have risen by almost 100,000 tonnes in the past week to 400,000 tonnes, while one storage firm said stocks were 100-200,000 tonnes more than normal for the time of year.
"There has been a surplus of fuel oil in the area which has been able to press the prices," he said.

Dutch oil consultant Pieter Kulsen said storage could have been even higher as enquiries space peaked recently, but noted that some trading companies had decided against storing because of either the desire to hike prices or the simple price disincentive to store.
Competition from Singapore and the U.S. have also driven down bunkers. There too, traders say, stocks have been higher than expected.
"We thought traders wouldn't want to see the inventories in the balance sheet at the end of the year, but the they have surprised us," said one storage firm in the ARA region.

In Europe, the market looks unlikely to tighten. Venezuelan imports are proceeding apace and Russian suppliers have continued to pump oil into northern Europe. Unlike last winter, the Russian government has not increased the export tariff on fuel oil. But ARA players probably erred on the side of caution and stocked up nonetheless.

Exports from the Baltic and the Black Sea in January, while down from November and December, were double their level in January 1996. Traders and brokers say they expect Russian exports to grow in February.
Shipowners are nonetheless not flaunting their delight.
"I would say it's still a sellers market. It's just a correction of the situation," said one.
"We're never happy with the price," said another.
-- Philip Blenkinsop, Amsterdam newsroom +31 20 504 5004
